question: What did Acme Corp say about their current workflow?

resolution.read_instruction: Extract everything the prospect (Acme) says about its current workflow, including how work is done today, tools and systems in use, pain points, bottlenecks, and manual steps.
assumptions: 'Acme Corp' is taken to refer to the catalogue company Acme Logistics (CALL-001), the only Acme entry.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: Handoffs between sales, onboarding and customer success. All of that is managed through spreadsheets and Slack reminders.
findings.context: Handoffs between sales, onboarding and customer success are managed through spreadsheets and Slack reminders, so renewal risks and implementation blockers are noticed late. — Core description of current workflow and main pain point

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: Sometimes a week. Sometimes we find out at the QBR
findings.context: Late detection sometimes means a week of delay, and sometimes issues are only found at the QBR. — Rachel quantifying how late problems are noticed

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: It's not that every step is manual. We have automation in places. The problem is the gaps between the automated pieces. Something runs, then nothing happens for four days, then a human notices.
findings.context: Acme has some automation, but the main problem is the gaps between automated pieces, where work stalls until a human notices. — Rachel explicitly corrects the assumption that every step is manual

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: The operational telemetry is weak. We can usually tell you something was late after the fact. We're much worse at answering why it was late, or which dependency failed
findings.context: Operational telemetry is weak: Acme can tell after the fact that something was late but cannot easily tell why, which dependency failed, or how often it recurs. — Rachel on measurement and visibility gaps

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: When things work, nobody notices. When something sticks, the escalation path depends entirely on who happens to see it. And people compensate — they build their own reminders, their own little spreadsheets, someone wrote a script once.
findings.context: Acme has automation nobody quite owns; when something breaks, escalation depends on who happens to see it, and people compensate with personal reminders, spreadsheets and scripts that leave with them. — Tom on ownership and key-person risk

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: We have at least two scripts running that I could not tell you the author of.
findings.context: At least three running scripts exist whose authors are unknown to the team. — Rachel said two; Tom corrected to three

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.context: The count of unowned scripts is three, not two. — Self-correction by Tom of Rachel's count

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: Earlier we described onboarding as standardised. That's what the deck says. In practice EMEA and North America use different milestone definitions.
findings.context: Onboarding is described as standardised in the deck, but EMEA and North America use different milestone definitions, so a single workflow diagram is misleading. — Tom correcting earlier statement made by the team

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: The process people describe and the process people run are not always the same thing.
findings.context: The documented process and the process actually run by staff differ. — Tom and Rachel agreeing on the gap between documented and actual process

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: Customer and commercial data, that's clear. Tasks and tickets, that's somewhere else. And then a lot of the actual context is in chat
findings.context: System of record varies by object: customer and commercial data is clear, tasks and tickets live elsewhere, and much of the actual context sits in chat. — Rachel on where process data lives

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: The data team uses it for a handful of back-office integrations. It works. But RevOps finds it too technical
findings.context: Acme already uses Workato: the data team uses it for back-office integrations, it works, but RevOps finds it too technical and avoids IT tickets for workflow changes. — Tom describing existing automation tooling

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: We've had integrations die because someone renamed a field or added a picklist value, and the automation just — didn't say anything.
findings.context: Integrations have failed silently when source schema changed (renamed field, new picklist value). — Tom describing a concrete failure mode of current automation

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: individual ownership is genuinely one of the reasons our current stuff breaks.
findings.context: Individual ownership of processes is one of the reasons Acme's current automation breaks, since people change roles constantly. — Tom on person-dependence

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: We've got expensive people doing coordination work because the systems don't carry enough process context.
findings.context: Acme pays for expensive staff to do coordination work because systems don't carry enough process context; maintenance scripts quietly consume engineer hours over time. — Rachel on cost of current approach; Tom on hidden engineering cost

draft.answer: Acme Logistics (Rachel Morgan, VP RevOps, and Tom Alvarez, Director of Customer Success) described a workflow run on spreadsheets and Slack reminders, with partial automation and gaps where work stalls [C1][C2]. Ownership is weak and relies on individuals and unowned scripts [C3]. Documented and actual processes differ, and visibility is poor [C4]. Existing tooling includes Workato, and integrations have failed silently [C5]. The cost shows up in staff time [C6].

claims.text: Rachel Morgan said handoffs between sales, onboarding and customer success are managed through spreadsheets and Slack reminders, so problems are noticed late: sometimes a week, sometimes only at the QBR.
Rachel said not every step is manual; Acme has some automation, but the problem is the gaps between automated pieces, where something runs, then nothing happens for four days until a human notices.

Tom Alvarez said some automation is not clearly owned, escalation depends on who happens to see a problem, and people build their own reminders, spreadsheets and scripts. Rachel said at least two scripts had unknown authors, and Tom corrected the count to three. Tom said individual ownership is one reason current automation breaks, because people change roles constantly.

Tom said onboarding is described as standardised in the deck, but EMEA and North America use different milestone definitions. He said the documented process and the process actually run are not always the same. Rachel said customer and commercial data has a clear system of record, but tasks and tickets live elsewhere and much context is in chat. Rachel also said operational telemetry is weak: Acme can tell something was late but not why or which dependency failed.

Tom said Acme already uses Workato: the data team uses it for back-office integrations and it works, but RevOps finds it too technical. Tom also said integrations have died silently when a field was renamed or a picklist value added.
Rachel said Acme has expensive people doing coordination work because systems don't carry enough process context.

conflicts.description: The deck describes onboarding as standardised, but Tom said in practice EMEA and North America use different milestone definitions.
Rachel said at least two scripts have unknown authors; Tom corrected it to three.

assumptions: 'Acme Corp' refers to Acme Logistics (CALL-001), the only Acme entry.
